findings.title: SQL injection via unvalidated @SortColumn
findings.explanation: @SortColumn is concatenated directly into the dynamic SQL text in the ORDER BY clause without validation or quoting. A caller can pass a value such as 'Name; DROP TABLE dbo.Products; --' or a subquery to execute arbitrary T-SQL under the procedure's security context. Parameterizing sp_executesql does not protect identifiers, so this is a real injection path.
findings.reason: Identifies the same SQL injection through concatenating @SortColumn into the ORDER BY clause without quoting or an allow-list.

findings.title: Leading-wildcard LIKE prevents index seeks
findings.explanation: The pattern '%' + @Search + '%' has a leading wildcard, so any index on Name can only be scanned, not seeked. On a large Products table this causes full scans on every search.
findings.reason: A substring search inherently needs a leading wildcard; this is the intended behavior, not a defect, and the remark is speculative advice.

findings.title: LIKE wildcard characters in user input are not escaped
findings.explanation: If @Search contains %, _ or [ characters, they are interpreted as LIKE wildcards rather than literal text, so searches for literal underscores or brackets return unexpected rows.
findings.reason: Wildcards %, _ and [ in @Search are not escaped, so literal searches return unexpected rows. This is a genuine but minor correctness issue.

findings.title: NULL input silently produces no results
findings.explanation: If @Search is NULL, @pattern becomes NULL and the LIKE predicate never matches, so the procedure returns an empty result with no error or warning. The same applies to a NULL @SortColumn, which makes @sql NULL and causes sp_executesql to do nothing silently.
findings.reason: A NULL @SortColumn makes @sql NULL, so sp_executesql silently does nothing and the procedure returns no result set and no error. This is a real silent-failure defect. NULL @Search returning nothing is expected SQL semantics.

findings.title: No error handling around dynamic SQL execution
findings.explanation: The procedure has no TRY...CATCH block and no validation of the dynamic SQL path. Any runtime error from the dynamic statement propagates to the caller without context, and the procedure gives no clear feedback for invalid sort requests.
findings.reason: Lack of TRY...CATCH is a generic best-practice remark. Propagating errors to the caller is acceptable, so this is not a concrete defect.

findings.title: Race condition on balance check (lost update / overdraft)
findings.explanation: The source balance is read into a variable at line 14-15 without a locking hint, then written back as @Balance - @Amount at line 24. Two concurrent transfers from the same account can both read the same balance, both pass the check, and both write results computed from that stale value. This can overdraw the account or lose one debit. Under READ COMMITTED, the read takes no update lock that would serialize these calls.
findings.reason: Describes the unlocked read followed by a write from the stale variable, which allows lost updates and overdrafts.

findings.title: No TRY/CATCH error handling and no XACT_ABORT
findings.explanation: The transaction has no BEGIN TRY / BEGIN CATCH block, and SET XACT_ABORT ON is not set. If a runtime error occurs between BEGIN TRANSACTION and COMMIT (for example a constraint violation or deadlock on the UPDATE or INSERT), the procedure may leave the transaction open or uncommitted. The caller then gets an unclear error, and locks can be held longer than intended. Also, the explicit ROLLBACK paths at lines 19 and 33 can fail if no transaction is active.
findings.reason: Names the missing TRY/CATCH and XACT_ABORT, and the resulting open transaction when a statement fails.

findings.title: Self-transfer is not rejected
findings.explanation: If @FromAccountId equals @ToAccountId, the procedure debits and then credits the same row, so the net change is zero, but it still writes a Transfers record for a transfer that did not happen. The procedure does not validate this input.
findings.reason: A self-transfer is not rejected and produces a bogus Transfers record. This is a genuine validation gap that no label covers.

findings.title: Destination account is validated after the source is debited
findings.explanation: The existence of @ToAccountId is only checked at line 31, after the source balance has already been updated. The code relies on rollback for correctness, which works but is fragile and does unnecessary write work for an invalid input. The check is also tied to @@ROWCOUNT from the second UPDATE only, which makes the logic harder to follow.
findings.reason: The destination check happens inside a transaction and is rolled back on failure, so the result is correct. The remark is a design preference, not a defect.

findings.title: NOT IN returns no rows if the subquery yields a NULL CustomerId
findings.explanation: If any row in dbo.Orders matching the year has a NULL CustomerId, the NOT IN predicate evaluates to UNKNOWN for every customer, so the procedure returns an empty result set. This silently gives wrong results whenever the Orders table contains such a row.
findings.reason: Identifies the NOT IN with NULL CustomerId problem that yields an empty result set.

findings.title: Non-sargable predicate on OrderDate
findings.explanation: Wrapping OrderDate in YEAR() prevents the optimizer from using an index seek on OrderDate and forces a scan of all order rows, which gets worse as the Orders table grows.
findings.reason: Identifies YEAR() on OrderDate as non-sargable, preventing an index seek.

findings.title: No supporting index for the anti-join
findings.explanation: The subquery filters Orders by OrderDate and reads CustomerId. Without an index leading on OrderDate (or on CustomerId with OrderDate included), the lookup for matching orders requires scanning the table.
findings.reason: Speculative advice to add an index; the schema is not shown, and the actual defect is the non-sargable predicate, which makes an index on OrderDate ineffective anyway.

findings.title: Cursor used for row-by-row price updates
findings.explanation: The price import is implemented with a cursor that issues one UPDATE per staging row. This is slow for large batches, holds locks for longer, and is harder to maintain than the equivalent set-based statement.
findings.reason: Same defect: row-by-row cursor UPDATE instead of a set-based join update, with the same lock and performance rationale.

findings.title: Cursor declared without explicit options
findings.explanation: The cursor does not specify LOCAL, FORWARD_ONLY or READ_ONLY. Its scope and behaviour then depend on database settings (for example, a global cursor default), and an updatable cursor may be created unnecessarily.
findings.reason: Missing LOCAL/FORWARD_ONLY options is a minor style or best-practice remark that has no real effect here, since the cursor is closed and deallocated in the same procedure.

findings.title: @@IDENTITY used to obtain the new log ID
findings.explanation: @@IDENTITY returns the last identity value generated in the session, from any scope. If a trigger on dbo.ImportLog inserts into another identity table, the wrong ID is returned and staging rows are linked to the wrong log entry.
findings.reason: Correctly identifies @@IDENTITY returning a trigger's identity value instead of SCOPE_IDENTITY().

findings.title: No TRY/CATCH error handling
findings.explanation: The procedure has no TRY...CATCH block. XACT_ABORT rolls back the transaction on error, but the caller gets no controlled error message, no context about which step failed, and the transaction state is never checked for an uncommittable state.
findings.reason: With XACT_ABORT ON, errors roll back the transaction and propagate to the caller. Missing TRY/CATCH is a style preference, not a defect.

findings.title: Batch can be imported more than once
findings.explanation: Nothing checks whether @BatchId has already been applied. Calling the procedure again with the same batch re-applies every price change and writes another ImportLog entry, which can overwrite newer prices with stale ones.
findings.reason: No idempotency guard: re-running the same BatchId reapplies stale prices and writes duplicate logs. This is a plausible genuine defect in an import procedure.

findings.title: Duplicate SKUs in a batch silently overwrite each other
findings.explanation: If staging.PriceChanges contains more than one row for the same Sku within a batch, each row is applied in turn and the last one processed wins. Nothing detects or reports the conflict, so the final price depends on row order.
findings.reason: Duplicate SKUs in a batch make the final price depend on cursor order with no detection. This is a real data-integrity concern.

findings.title: Possible missing index on staging filter column
findings.explanation: The cursor query filters staging.PriceChanges on BatchId, and the later UPDATE filters on the same column. Without an index on BatchId this causes table scans as staging grows. The UPDATE on dbo.Products filtered by Sku also depends on an index on Sku.
findings.reason: Speculative index advice that cannot be verified from the code, and no evidence of a missing index.

findings.title: OUTPUT parameter not reset when no customer matches
findings.explanation: A SELECT that returns no rows leaves the target variable unchanged. If the caller passes a non-NULL @CustomerId, the IF @CustomerId IS NULL check at line 19 is false, so the procedure takes the UPDATE branch and modifies whichever customer has that caller-supplied ID. The new customer is never inserted, and the wrong record can be overwritten.
findings.reason: Valid: @CustomerId is an OUTPUT parameter that can carry a caller-supplied value in. A SELECT that matches no rows leaves it unchanged, so a non-NULL input sends the procedure into the UPDATE branch for the wrong customer. The fix is to set @CustomerId = NULL before the SELECT.

findings.title: Email is validated after trimming but stored and matched untrimmed
findings.explanation: Line 10 trims whitespace only for the empty-check. The untrimmed @Email is then used in the lookup at line 17 and the insert at line 21. Input such as ' a@b.com' is stored with the leading space, and later lookups for 'a@b.com' miss it, creating duplicate customers.
findings.reason: Valid: the email is trimmed only for the emptiness check, then matched and stored untrimmed, so padded input produces duplicate or missed customers. This is a genuine inconsistency.

findings.title: Serializable range locking with no visible unique index on Email
findings.explanation: WITH (UPDLOCK, HOLDLOCK) acquires key-range locks on the Email lookup. Concurrent calls for new emails can deadlock, since each takes the range lock and then tries to insert. Without a unique index on Email, the lookup may also scan the table and escalate locks. The procedure's correctness depends entirely on this locking because nothing in the code enforces uniqueness.
findings.reason: UPDLOCK, HOLDLOCK is the standard safe upsert pattern and is correct here. The finding is speculative about an index that is not visible, and the deadlock claim is overstated because UPDLOCK serializes concurrent callers on the same key.  ,

findings.title: No TRY/CATCH or explicit rollback around the transaction
findings.explanation: XACT_ABORT ON rolls back on most errors, but the procedure gives the caller no structured error handling. Errors such as unique-key violations are re-raised with no context, and the transaction is not rolled back explicitly if an error is caught by the caller. The procedure also does not check @@TRANCOUNT, so it behaves unpredictably when called inside an outer transaction.
findings.reason: SET XACT_ABORT ON already rolls back the transaction on error, so the missing TRY/CATCH is not a defect. The claims about outer transactions and context are speculative best-practice advice.

findings.title: NULL @Name is accepted and can overwrite existing names
findings.explanation: Only @Email is validated. A NULL @Name passed to the UPDATE at line 29 sets Name to NULL for an existing customer, and the insert at line 21 may fail if Name is NOT NULL. The procedure has no defined behavior for a missing name.
findings.reason: Valid: a NULL @Name silently overwrites an existing customer's name with NULL on update, and the procedure defines no behavior for a missing name. This is a real data-loss risk.

findings.title: Rows with NULL Status are silently excluded
findings.explanation: The predicate o.Status <> N'Cancelled' evaluates to UNKNOWN when Status is NULL, so orders with no status are dropped from the revenue totals without any signal. If NULL is a valid state for unprocessed orders, revenue and order counts are understated.
findings.reason: The NULL behavior of <> is real, but it is speculative: the finding itself says 'if NULL is a valid state'. Status is likely NOT NULL, and nothing in the code shows NULL is valid. No defect established.

findings.title: Month expression duplicated in SELECT and GROUP BY
findings.explanation: DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(o.OrderDate), MONTH(o.OrderDate), 1) is repeated in the select list and the GROUP BY. Keeping the two copies in sync is error-prone and the expression is harder to read.
findings.reason: Repeating the expression in SELECT and GROUP BY is required in T-SQL and is standard practice; column aliases cannot be used in GROUP BY. This is a style remark, not a defect.

findings.title: Hardcoded magic numbers for valid year range and error code
findings.explanation: The bounds 2000 and 2100 and the error number 50030 are embedded directly in the validation. Changing the accepted range requires a code change and the values carry no documented meaning.
findings.reason: Magic-number complaint is a style preference. The validation bounds and error code are clear in context and do not cause a bug.

findings.title: Unencoded query parameter in URL
findings.explanation: The trimmed search term is interpolated directly into the URL without encodeURIComponent. Characters such as '&', '#', '+' or '=' change the request's meaning, so a query like 'a&admin=true' injects extra parameters, and '#' truncates the query string entirely.
findings.reason: Identifies the unencoded term in the URL at line 23 and the broken or injected query parameters.

findings.title: Effect has no cleanup; timer and request are never cancelled
findings.explanation: The effect creates an AbortController and a setTimeout but returns no cleanup function. When query or delayMs changes or the component unmounts, the pending timer still fires and the in-flight fetch is never aborted. Responses for stale queries can then overwrite results for the current query, and state updates can happen after unmount.
findings.reason: Reports the missing effect cleanup, so timers and requests are never cancelled and stale responses can overwrite newer results.

findings.title: Unvalidated type assertion on API response
findings.explanation: response.json() returns Promise<any>, and the result is asserted as Product[] without any runtime check. If the API returns an unexpected shape, the component will store invalid data and downstream code may fail at runtime.
findings.reason: The cast of response.json() to Product[] is a common TypeScript pattern. Runtime validation is a best-practice suggestion, not a defect in this code.

findings.title: Stale error is not cleared when the query becomes too short
findings.explanation: The short-query branch clears results but leaves any previous error set. The hook can therefore return results: [] alongside a stale error message from an earlier failed search.
findings.reason: The short-query branch resets results but leaves the old error set, so the hook can return empty results with a stale error. This is a genuine minor bug.

findings.title: Missing explicit return type on exported hook
findings.explanation: The exported hook has no return type annotation, so its public contract is inferred from the implementation. Changes to the returned shape can then ripple silently into consumers.
findings.reason: A missing explicit return type is a style preference. The inferred type is accurate.

findings.title: taxCents returns fractional cents
findings.explanation: The function divides by 100 without rounding, so it can return values like 123.45 for a function named in cents. Callers that add this to integer cent totals will propagate fractional amounts, and formatCents or any money storage would then carry rounding errors.
findings.reason: Identifies that taxCents returns unrounded fractional cents at line 26, the same defect as label 1.

findings.title: parseQuantity accepts NaN and non-integers
findings.explanation: Number(input) returns NaN for inputs like 'abc', and NaN fails both comparisons in the range check, so NaN is returned as a valid quantity. Inputs like '2.5' also pass the range check and return a fractional quantity, which would corrupt subtotalCents.
findings.reason: Describes NaN and fractional quantities passing the range check in parseQuantity, the same as label 2.

findings.title: percentOff is not validated
findings.explanation: applyCoupon does not check that percentOff is between 0 and 100. A negative value increases the price (the Math.max clamp only prevents negatives at zero), and a value above 100 produces a discount larger than the subtotal, which is only hidden by clamping to 0. Invalid coupon data is silently accepted.
findings.reason: Coupon percentOff validation is speculative input validation on typed data from the caller; the code is not defective as written, and the claim that a negative value is a bug is a stretch of the function's contract.

findings.title: Mutable data shapes for value objects
findings.explanation: CartItem and Coupon are plain mutable interfaces, so callers can change quantity or prices after validation or during calculation. Nothing in the type system prevents accidental mutation of cart data.
findings.reason: Suggesting readonly interfaces is a style preference and not a defect.

findings.title: Currency and locale are loosely typed
findings.explanation: currency is inferred as string, so any value is accepted at compile time. Invalid codes make Intl.NumberFormat throw a RangeError at runtime, and cents / 100 is applied without any integer check on the input.
findings.reason: Loose currency typing is a preference; Intl throwing on an invalid code is reasonable behavior, not a defect.

findings.title: No validation of cart item values
findings.explanation: subtotalCents trusts unitPriceCents and quantity without checking that they are non-negative integers. Negative, NaN, or fractional values flow silently into totals and discounts.
findings.reason: Speculative defensive validation of typed inputs in subtotalCents; the real issue (quantity parsing) is covered elsewhere.

findings.title: Password and email logged to the console
findings.explanation: console.debug logs the raw password (and email) on every sign-in attempt. Anyone with access to browser devtools, error-reporting integrations that capture console output, or shared machines can read user credentials.
findings.reason: Identifies the console.debug call that logs the password and email at line 19, the same defect as the label.

findings.title: Unvalidated returnUrl used for redirect (open redirect)
findings.explanation: The returnUrl query parameter is passed directly to window.location.assign without validation. An attacker can craft a sign-in link such as /signin?returnUrl=https://evil.example that sends the user to a phishing site after successful login. The file already defines safeReturnUrl for this purpose but it is not used here.
findings.reason: Identifies the open redirect from passing returnUrl unvalidated to window.location.assign, and notes safeReturnUrl goes unused.

findings.title: Network failures are not handled with a clear error
findings.explanation: If fetch rejects (offline, DNS failure, aborted request), the raw TypeError propagates to the caller with no user-facing message. The error handling only covers HTTP status codes.
findings.reason: Letting a fetch rejection propagate as an error is normal behavior; the caller can handle it. This is a speculative preference, not a defect.

findings.title: Default parameter reads window at call time
findings.explanation: The origin default uses window.location.origin, which makes safeReturnUrl depend on a browser global. It cannot be used in SSR or Node-based tests without a window object, and the dependency is hidden in the signature.
findings.reason: The default parameter is evaluated at call time and the origin can be overridden by passing an argument. This is a style remark with no real defect.

findings.title: Untyped response handling and magic values
findings.explanation: The response body is never parsed or typed, and the status code and parameter name "returnUrl" are inline literals. This makes the contract with the API implicit and fragile to change.
findings.reason: The function does not need the response body, and inline literals here are a style preference rather than a defect.

findings.title: SQL injection via string concatenation
findings.explanation: The query concatenates the raw req.params.id into the SQL string. The earlier parseInt validation only checks the parsed value, so an input like "1 OR 1=1" passes validation (parseInt returns 1) and the unparsed string is injected into the query. This allows arbitrary SQL execution and data exfiltration.
findings.reason: Identifies the concatenated req.params.id on line 15 and explains why the parseInt check does not protect the query, which is the SQL injection label.

findings.title: Lenient integer parsing accepts malformed ids
findings.explanation: Number.parseInt accepts partial numeric strings such as "12abc" or "1.9" and returns 12 or 1, so invalid input is silently accepted and a different order may be fetched than the one requested.
findings.reason: parseInt accepting '12abc' is a real looseness in validation. It is minor but genuine, since a different order than the one requested may be fetched. The underlying injection is covered by a different label.

findings.title: req.user accessed without authentication guarantee
findings.explanation: req.user is not part of the Express Request type unless augmented, and it is undefined when no auth middleware ran or the user is anonymous. Accessing req.user.id will throw a TypeError, and in this file there is no check that the caller is authenticated before cancelling an order.
findings.reason: req.user is used without any auth guard or type augmentation in the file, so it can throw a TypeError. A reasonable reviewer would flag this, though it is somewhat speculative since auth middleware likely exists elsewhere.

findings.title: Ambiguous status code for cancel failures
findings.explanation: Returning 409 when rowCount is not 1 conflates several cases: the order does not exist, belongs to another customer, is not pending, or rowCount is null. The client cannot tell them apart, and the pg typing of rowCount as possibly null is not handled explicitly.
findings.reason: Using 409 for all cancel failures is a design preference. It does not hide a bug, and not exposing why the cancel failed is arguably intentional, since it avoids leaking order existence.

findings.title: Error details and stack traces leaked to clients
findings.explanation: The error handler returns String(err) and err.stack in the JSON response. This exposes internal implementation details, file paths, and database error messages to any client, which aids attackers.
findings.reason: The error handler on line 40 returns String(err) and the stack trace to the client, which is the information leak label.

findings.title: Pool created without error listener
findings.explanation: A pg Pool emits 'error' when an idle client fails, for example after a database restart. With no listener attached, this unhandled event can crash the Node process.
findings.reason: pg Pool emits 'error' on idle client failures. Without a listener, the event is unhandled and can crash the process. This is a genuine robustness defect.

findings.title: Untyped database results
findings.explanation: pool.query is used without a generic type, so rows is any and rows[0] is returned unchecked. There is no interface describing the order shape, so type safety is lost from the database boundary to the response.
findings.reason: Missing generics on the query result is a typing and style preference and not a functional defect.

findings.title: Missing explicit return type on exported function
findings.explanation: errorHandler has no return type annotation, and the exported function signature is not fully documented. Relying on inference weakens the API contract.
findings.reason: A missing explicit return type on the handler is a style nitpick with no practical impact.

findings.title: Month is off by one in toDate
findings.explanation: CalendarDay documents months as 1-12, but the JavaScript Date constructor expects 0-11. Passing month directly to new Date(year, month, day) shifts every date into the following month. For example, {year: 2024, month: 1, day: 15} produces February 15, 2024.
findings.reason: Reports the month off-by-one in toDate, passing a 1-based month to the Date constructor.

findings.title: day field is populated from getDay() (weekday) instead of getDate() (day of month)
findings.explanation: Date.getDay() returns the day of the week (0-6, Sunday-Saturday), not the day of the month. fromDate therefore returns a wrong day value for almost every date, and this breaks addDays, compare and every other consumer of the result.
findings.reason: Reports getDay() being used instead of getDate() in fromDate.

findings.title: addDays inherits the month offset bug and produces wrong results
findings.explanation: addDays builds its Date through toDate, which shifts the month by one. Date arithmetic is therefore performed on the wrong calendar date. Combined with the getDay bug in fromDate, the returned CalendarDay is incorrect. For example, adding 1 day to {2024, 1, 31} computes from March 2 rather than January 31.
findings.reason: Describes ts-06-calendar-days#1 but at lines 18-19, outside the window. addDays is wrong because of the toDate month shift, which the label names as a consequence. The fromDate getDay bug is only mentioned as an extra contributor.

findings.title: daysInMonth returns the length of the previous month
findings.explanation: new Date(year, month, 0) yields the last day of the 0-indexed month month-1, which is the 1-based month-1. For a 1-based month, daysInMonth(2024, 2) returns 31 (January) instead of 29 (February).
findings.reason: daysInMonth is correct. new Date(year, month, 0) with a 1-based month is day 0 of the next month, which is the last day of the requested month. daysInMonth(2024, 2) returns 29.

findings.title: isWeekend computes the weekday from a wrongly shifted date
findings.explanation: isWeekend calls toDate, which shifts the month by one, so the weekday is computed for a different date than the one passed in. Weekend results are wrong for many inputs.
findings.reason: Describes ts-06-calendar-days#1 but at lines 27-28, outside the window. isWeekend gives wrong results because toDate shifts the month, which the label explicitly lists as a consequence.

findings.title: CalendarDay fields are mutable and unvalidated
findings.explanation: The interface does not mark its fields readonly, and nothing enforces the documented 1-12 month range or valid day ranges. Invalid values silently roll over inside Date.
findings.reason: Missing readonly and input validation is a design preference, not a defect in this code.

findings.title: delayMs is not validated before being passed to setInterval
findings.explanation: The effect only checks for null. Negative, NaN, Infinity, or fractional values are passed straight to setInterval, which coerces them silently (for example, to a minimum of about 1ms or 0ms). A zero or near-zero delay can run the callback at a very high rate and cause heavy CPU use or a frozen UI.
findings.reason: The hook's contract is a numeric delay or null. Passing 0 or a negative delay is a caller choice and the browser handles it predictably, so omitting validation is not a defect here.

findings.title: Effect has a bare return on one path and a function return on another
findings.explanation: The effect returns nothing in the null case and a cleanup function otherwise. With noImplicitReturns enabled in tsconfig, TypeScript reports 'Not all code paths return a value' (TS7030). The inconsistency also makes the control flow harder to read.
findings.reason: The bare `return;` in an effect is the standard pattern. TS7030 does not fire for a bare return, so the claim is wrong, and the rest is a style preference.

findings.title: Errors thrown by the callback are not handled
findings.explanation: If saved.current() throws, the error is raised from the timer callback and goes uncaught. The interval keeps running, so the same error can repeat on every tick with no context about the hook that caused it.
findings.reason: Uncaught callback errors propagate to the global handler, as with any setInterval. Handling them is the caller's job, and swallowing them in the hook would be wrong, so this is speculative advice rather than a defect.

findings.title: Unbounded array allocation in splitCents
findings.explanation: The only check on `parts` is that it is a positive integer (line 23). A large value such as 1e9 makes Array.from on line 28 allocate a huge array and can exhaust memory. Values above 2^32-1 throw a RangeError from the Array constructor rather than the function's own validation error. If `parts` comes from user input, this is a denial-of-service risk.
findings.reason: The output length equals the caller-requested number of parts, so the allocation is inherent to the function's contract. Nothing in this file shows untrusted input reaching it, so this is speculative.

findings.title: Currency and locale are unvalidated strings
findings.explanation: `currency` and `locale` are plain strings passed directly to Intl.NumberFormat. An invalid ISO 4217 code or malformed BCP 47 tag makes the constructor throw a RangeError with a message that does not mention this function. The signature also gives no hint of the expected values.
findings.reason: Intl.NumberFormat already throws a RangeError for an invalid currency or locale, which is reasonable behavior. Wrapping it for a nicer message is a style preference, not a defect.

findings.title: Intl.NumberFormat constructed on every call
findings.explanation: A new Intl.NumberFormat is created for each formatting call. Construction is comparatively expensive, so formatting many amounts in a loop wastes CPU.
findings.reason: Caching formatters is a micro-optimization with no evidence it matters here. The code is correct as written, so this is only a preference remark.
